claims.text: Adding approximately 0.1 wt% yttrium to a high-entropy-alloy bond coat will improve thermal-barrier-coating durability and reliability.
Yttrium doping will enable in situ formation of a stable, adherent oxide scale.
The untreated high-entropy-alloy bond coat has a complex concentrated phase structure.
An untreated high-entropy-alloy bond coat undergoes conventional oxidation and eventual oxide-scale degradation during thermal cycling.
The proposed intervention should remain effective under cyclic oxidizing conditions at 1200–1315°C.
Yttrium produces a modified interfacial oxide scale likely containing yttrium-alumina constituents.
The yttrium-modified oxide scale has greater adhesion and lower defect density.
Yttrium segregates to the bond-coat surface during oxidation.
Surface-segregated yttrium stabilizes the growing oxide by reducing defect formation.
Yttrium eases thermal-expansion mismatch at the coating interface.
The proposed mechanism creates a more continuous and adherent oxide that better resists spallation during thermal cycling.
The yttrium-doped bond coat will have lower oxidation weight gain than the untreated bond coat.
The yttrium-doped bond coat will exhibit a recession rate below 0.25 μm/h.
The yttrium-doped bond coat will improve adhesion between the bond coat and the thermal-barrier coating relative to the untreated baseline.
Untreated high-entropy-alloy bond coats typically form non-ideal oxide scales, have higher recession rates, and cause premature thermal-barrier-coating spallation.
The benefit is expected to be limited to approximately 0.1 wt% yttrium and the specified cyclic high-temperature regime.
Changing the yttrium level or substantially changing the thermal or environmental conditions may eliminate the predicted improvement.
Direct experimental evidence connecting yttrium-doped high-entropy-alloy bond coats to improved thermal-barrier-coating durability is limited.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% reduction in recession rate and spallation, together with improved adhesion, relative to an undoped control would falsify the hypothesis.
